title: Logical Equivalence and De Morgan's Laws
short: Two statements are equivalent when their truth tables match: ¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q, and P → Q ≡ ¬P ∨ Q.
trouble: Students negate "P and Q" as "not P and not Q," or treat a conditional as equivalent to its converse instead of its contrapositive.

blocks.html: Two statements can look different and still say the same thing. With the conditional and the truth tables you already have, you can test this precisely, and a few standard equivalences then let you rewrite statements without building a table every time.

$A$ and $B$ are logically equivalent, written $A \equiv B$, when they have the same truth value in every row of the truth table. The most used ones are De Morgan's laws, $ eg(P \wedge Q) \equiv eg P \vee eg Q$ and $ eg(P \vee Q) \equiv eg P \wedge eg Q$, and the conditional laws $P o Q \equiv eg P \vee Q \equiv eg Q o eg P$.

Why does the "and" turn into an "or" when you negate it? $P \wedge Q$ claims two things at once. To deny it, you only need one of them to fail: "not both" means "at least one is false," which is $
eg P \vee 
eg Q$. In the same way, $P \vee Q$ claims at least one thing, and denying it means neither holds: $
eg P \wedge 
eg Q$. For the conditional, $P 	o Q$ is false only when $P$ is true and $Q$ is false; $
eg P \vee Q$ is false in exactly the same row, so they match everywhere.

blocks.title: Checking an equivalence with a table
blocks.q: Is $P \to Q$ equivalent to its converse $Q \to P$? Is it equivalent to its contrapositive $\neg Q \to \neg P$?
steps: $P \to Q$ has column T, F, T, T (rows TT, TF, FT, FF).
$Q \to P$ is false only when $Q$ is true and $P$ is false, row FT: column T, T, F, T. The columns differ, so the converse is not equivalent.

blocks.title: Negating in English
blocks.q: Negate "The store is open and the lights are on."
steps:
The statement is $P \wedge Q$, so its negation is $
eg(P \wedge Q) \equiv 
eg P \vee 
eg Q$.
In words: "The store is not open, or the lights are not on."
The tempting answer "The store is not open and the lights are not on" is too strong: it says both fail, but one failure is already enough.
blocks.a: The store is not open, or the lights are not on.

blocks.html: Two common slips. First, negating "$P$ and $Q$" as "not $P$ and not $Q$"; the negation is "not $P$ or not $Q$." Second, treating a conditional as equivalent to its converse. "If it rains, the ground is wet" does not mean "if the ground is wet, it rained" (a sprinkler can wet the ground). Check by finding one row where the two statements differ; that settles it.
